result: The experimental setup consisted of a 30-electrode EEG array positioned over multiple cortical areas in both hemispheres, with biphasic electrical stimulation pulses (200 μs/phase, 10-100 μA amplitude) delivered via a bipolar electrode.
evaluation: Claims C21 and C22 describe the methodological setup for the experiments. These are straightforward descriptions of the experimental apparatus shown in Figure 1A and 1C, with no apparent inconsistencies or missing information.

result: Deep layer (5/6) stimulation evoked ERPs with two prominent peaks at ~25 ms and ~180 ms post-stimulation, while superficial layer (2/3) stimulation preserved only the early component. Deep stimulation produced significantly larger ERP magnitude (6.2±0.9 SD·s) compared to superficial stimulation (3.3±0.8 SD·s, p=0.0354), though ERP duration differences were not significant (p=0.0843).
evaluation: Claims C23-C26 are well-supported by experimental data in Figures 1C-F with appropriate statistical tests. The p-value for duration (0.0843) correctly indicates non-significance, while the magnitude difference is statistically significant. Sample sizes are adequate (N=12 superficial, N=18 deep).

result: The first ERP peak amplitude decays systematically with distance from the stimulation site and eventually flips polarity, likely reflecting volume conduction, while the second component shows a different spatial pattern suggesting a different mechanistic origin.
evaluation: Claims C27-C28 are supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The inference about volume conduction for the first peak is reasonable given the systematic decay and polarity flip. The different pattern for the second component appropriately suggests distinct mechanisms, setting up later findings about thalamic involvement.

result: Superficial MOs stimulation evoked local responses followed by 94.2±16.1 ms quiescence with minimal responses in other areas, while deep MOs stimulation evoked a triphasic pattern (initial excitation at 38.1±4.2 Hz, 125.0±5.5 ms quiescence, rebound excitation at 7.9±0.7 Hz) with approximately three times more cortical neurons responding significantly compared to superficial stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C29-C32 are well-supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 4. The quantitative measurements of firing rates and quiescence durations are clearly presented. The three-fold difference in neuronal recruitment is a key finding distinguishing deep from superficial stimulation effects.

result: Superficial stimulation significantly modulated local LFP, CSD, and spiking (p=0.0313 for all) and LFP/CSD in non-stimulated areas (p=0.0078), but did not evoke spiking outside the stimulated area (p=0.7422). Deep stimulation evoked significantly larger responses locally (p=1.221E-4) and in non-stimulated regions (p=3.052E-5), including significant spiking outside the stimulated area.
evaluation: Claims C33-C38 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3D with appropriate statistical tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank with Benjamini-Hochberg correction). Sample sizes are adequate (N=6 superficial, N=14 deep stimulated regions). The key finding that only deep stimulation evokes widespread cortical spiking is well-established.

result: During initial excitation (2-25 ms), only 0.5% of neurons in non-stimulated cortex were modulated versus 17.8% in stimulated cortex. In the off period (25-150 ms), few neurons showed increased spiking (0.4%), but 18/22 subjects showed decreased spiking, with some non-stimulated areas showing decreases only with deep stimulation (10.1%). During rebound (150-300 ms), all 16 deep stimulation subjects showed significant rebound in stimulated cortex versus only 1/6 superficial subjects, with 6/16 deep subjects showing rebound in non-stimulated areas versus 0/7 superficial subjects.
evaluation: Claims C39-C46 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4 across 24 animals. The temporal analysis across three windows (initial, off, rebound) is methodologically sound. The stark differences between deep and superficial stimulation in recruiting distant neurons are clearly demonstrated. Statistical corrections for multiple comparisons were appropriately applied (Benjamini-Hochberg).

result: The triphasic cortical spiking pattern was replicated in thalamic nuclei (SM-TH) with deep stimulation, showing brief excitation (22.3±3.2 Hz), 74.6±15.5 ms suppression, and rebound excitation (14.7±1.0 Hz) characterized by burst firing. SM-TH neurons were eight times more likely to be modulated by deep versus superficial stimulation (37.9±20.6% vs 5.0±4.1%, p=0.0037), with deep stimulation having significantly higher burst probability (median 0.12 vs 0, p=0.0258).
evaluation: Claims C47-C51 are well-supported by data in Figures 2F and 5A-C. The definition of bursting (≥2 spikes with <4 ms ISI preceded by ≥100 ms silence) is standard and appropriately cited. Statistical tests are appropriate (t-test, Mann-Whitney U). The eight-fold difference in modulation is striking and statistically significant.

result: During initial excitation, cortical neurons spiked first (4.4±0.9 ms) followed by thalamic neurons (11.4±2.8 ms, 6.9 ms difference, p=4.838E-6). During rebound, this relationship reversed: thalamic neurons spiked first (148.2±21.2 ms) followed by cortical neurons (184.2±17.3 ms, -36.0 ms difference, p=2.136E-4).
evaluation: Claims C52-C53 are strongly supported by data in Figures 5E-F with highly significant paired t-tests (N=13). The reversal of temporal relationships between initial and rebound periods is a key finding supporting the cortico-thalamo-cortical loop hypothesis. The latency differences are consistent with synaptic transmission and axonal conduction delays.

result: A pronounced current sink at the MOs layer 2/3-5 border coincided with thalamic rebound burst timing (~180 ms, N=9, p<0.05). EEG correlated more strongly with deep versus superficial layer CSD. Trial-by-trial correlations showed: thalamic burst fraction correlated with cortical firing rate (8/13 mice, r=0.4±0.04), cortical firing correlated with late ERP component (9/13 mice, r=0.5±0.04), and late ERP component strongly correlated with thalamic bursting (13/13 mice, r=0.5±0.07).
evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by data in Figure 6 and supplements. The CSD analysis appropriately identifies current sinks indicating synaptic input. The trial-by-trial correlation analysis is methodologically sound and provides strong evidence linking thalamic bursting to the late ERP component. The fact that 13/13 mice showed significant correlation between late ERP and thalamic bursting is particularly compelling.

result: Behavioral state modulated ERPs and neural responses. The second ERP component was diminished during running and absent during anesthesia, with significant decreases in ERP duration (Q(2)=15.6, p=4.002E-4) and magnitude (Q(2)=17.4, p=1.656E-4). Baseline firing rates were higher during running and lower during anesthesia in both cortex and thalamus. Initial excitation latencies were unchanged across states, but rebound latencies were earlier during running (state effect: F[2,24]=31.4, p=2.020E-7). Thalamic burst probability decreased from 0.1 during quiet wakefulness to effectively zero during running and anesthesia (Q[2]=18.6, p=9.142E-5). Thalamic activity preceded cortical activity during rebound in both waking states, with quiet wakefulness characterized by thalamic burst firing correlating with increased cortical spiking and higher ERP magnitudes.
evaluation: Claims C59-C66 are well-supported by comprehensive data in Figure 7 (N=17 animals for most analyses, N=13 for paired cortex-thalamus). Appropriate statistical tests were used (Friedman test for non-parametric data, RM ANOVA for parametric). The state-dependent modulation of thalamic bursting and its correlation with ERP features is a key finding. The authors appropriately note uncertainty about whether 'quiet wakefulness' might include drowsiness/sleep.

result: PCIST was significantly higher during awake versus anesthetized states in all subjects (45.5±3.6 vs 16.5±2.4, p=2.508E-11, N=31). PCIST was significantly lower for superficial versus deep stimulation (35.6±4.8 vs 52.7±4.4, p=0.0179). Across states, PCIST was highest during quiet wakefulness (55.2±10.3), lower during running (39.9±7.7), and lowest during anesthesia (14.0±5.8, F[2,14]=28.3, p=1.202E-5, N=8). PCIST recovered to near pre-anesthesia levels within 30 min after isoflurane cessation but did not increase further in the subsequent 30 min (F[3,18]=11.6, p=1.804E-4, N=13).
evaluation: Claims C67-C70 are well-supported by data in Figure 8 with appropriate statistical tests. The PCIST metric appropriately captures spatiotemporal complexity. The finding that PCIST is highest during quiet wakefulness, intermediate during running, and lowest during anesthesia is consistent with the underlying neural dynamics (particularly thalamic bursting). The recovery data provides additional validation. Sample sizes are adequate for all comparisons.

result: Superficial stimulation produces brief excitation followed by 44.3±16.4 ms silence in local cortical neurons without thalamic involvement, a pattern seen across species and reminiscent of bistability in deep sleep and unconscious patients. Deep stimulation produces a triphasic pattern (brief excitation, 127.8±4.1 ms silence, rebound excitation) in cortical and thalamic neurons, with similar rebound latencies reported in other studies.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 summarize key experimental findings and appropriately contextualize them with extensive citations to prior literature. The comparison to bistability in unconscious states is reasonable given the down-state characteristics. The consistency with prior studies strengthens the findings.

result: The cortical down-state may result from excitatory-inhibitory imbalance, refractory neurons, and/or lack of thalamic input. Strong thalamic recruitment 6.7 ms after cortical spiking is consistent with direct cortico-thalamic projections. The thalamic response pattern (brief excitation, 74.6±15.5 ms quiescence, burst firing) is consistent with prior studies and likely involves low-threshold Ca2+ spikes following hyperpolarization, potentially due to cortical down-state or disynaptic inhibition via reticular neurons.
evaluation: Claims C75-C79 mix supported observations (C76-C78) with speculative mechanistic explanations (C75, C79). While the timing data and consistency with prior work are solid, the authors appropriately acknowledge they cannot distinguish between proposed mechanisms (cortical down-state vs. reticular inhibition). The speculation is reasonable and well-grounded in cited literature, but definitive mechanistic validation would require additional experiments (e.g., optogenetic manipulation of specific cell types).

result: Thalamic bursting preceded cortical rebound by 37.0 ms, comparable to prior studies. The bursts are compatible with thalamic relay neurons exciting cortical targets. While spontaneous thalamic bursting occurs across various states, evoked rebound bursting occurred during quiet wakefulness but not running or isoflurane anesthesia, consistent with movement offset-related bursting and isoflurane's effects on low-threshold Ca2+ spikes. This does not contradict reports of bursting under other anesthetics (pentobarbital, ketamine/xylazine) or NREM sleep, which likely affect thalamic neurons differently.
evaluation: Claims C80-C86 are well-supported by experimental data and appropriately contextualized with extensive citations. The state-dependent nature of evoked thalamic bursting is a key finding. The authors appropriately reconcile their findings with prior literature showing bursting in other unconscious states by noting anesthetic-specific effects. The mechanistic explanation for isoflurane's effects is supported by citations.

result: Cortical firing rates increased from 3.3±0.2 Hz (quiet wakefulness) to 5.0±0.5 Hz (running) and decreased to 1.1±0.2 Hz (anesthesia). SM-TH rates increased from 9.4±1.5 Hz to 16.8±1.6 Hz (running) and decreased to 0.8±0.4 Hz (anesthesia). Evoked thalamic burst probability decreased from 9.5% (quiet wakefulness) to effectively zero (running and anesthesia). Stimulus-evoked thalamic bursts during quiet wakefulness result in longer, higher amplitude ERPs, consistent with prior studies showing thalamic bursts robustly activate cortical neurons. Greater thalamic bursting correlates with larger late ERP components.
evaluation: Claims C87-C92 are well-supported by data in Figures 7 and 6—figure supplement 2A, with appropriate statistical tests and extensive citations to prior literature. The state-dependent modulation of baseline firing rates and burst probability provides a mechanistic explanation for ERP differences across states. The consistency with prior studies on thalamic burst effects strengthens the interpretation.

result: PCIST values were higher during awake versus anesthetized states (quiet wakefulness 55.2±10.3, active wakefulness 39.9±7.7, anesthesia 14.0±5.8), consistent with prior human and rodent studies. ERPs are shorter and PCIST lower during active versus quiet wakefulness, possibly due to lower thalamic burst probability. All subjects showed higher PCIST during active wakefulness versus anesthesia. The PCIST pattern across states suggests an optimal network state maximizing complexity in mice, reminiscent of the inverted-U arousal-performance relationship.
evaluation: Claims C93-C96 are supported by data in Figure 8D with appropriate statistics (N=8, F[2,14]=28.3, p=1.202E-5) and citations to prior work. The inference about thalamic bursting as a mechanism (C94) is reasonable given the correlational data but remains somewhat speculative. The inverted-U interpretation (C96) is an interesting hypothesis supported by the data pattern and appropriately cited, though it would benefit from additional validation.

result: Studies indicate layer 5 pyramidal neurons and cortico-cortical feedback to infragranular pyramidal apical dendrites play critical roles in consciousness. The findings of shorter, less complex ERPs and reduced CTC circuit effectiveness during isoflurane anesthesia are compatible with studies on neuronal correlates of consciousness.
evaluation: Claims C97-C98 appropriately contextualize the findings within the consciousness literature. The authors appropriately note their study was not designed as a classical perceived vs. non-perceived paradigm but that their findings are compatible with such work. The interpretation is reasonable and appropriately cautious.

result: Mouse ERPs show two prominent components (25 and 180 ms) not apparent in human TMS-evoked EEG. Mouse brains (0.5 cm³, 71 million neurons) differ dramatically from human brains (1200 cm³, 86 billion neurons). Mouse neocortex (0.8-1 mm thick, 14 million neurons) differs from human neocortex (2.5-3.0 mm thick, 16 billion neurons). Mice have more layer 5 extratelencephalic and layer 6 corticothalamic neurons compared to primates, which have more layer 2/3 intratelencephalic neurons. This is consistent with pronounced cortico-thalamic activation and little widespread cortico-cortical activation in mice.
evaluation: Claims C99-C103 appropriately discuss species differences with accurate anatomical data from cited sources. The cellular composition differences (C102) from Bakken et al., 2021 provide a plausible explanation for the observed functional differences (C103). The interpretation linking cellular composition to functional observations is reasonable and appropriately cautious.

result: Electrical stimulation directly activates axons leading to antidromic/orthodromic propagation, while TMS excites neurons mainly trans-synaptically. Despite these differences, both stimulation in awake humans and mice evoke suppression of high frequencies (presumed off period) near the stimulation site, highlighting the role of perturbational technique in complexity measurements.
evaluation: Claims C104-C107 appropriately discuss methodological differences between electrical stimulation and TMS with appropriate citations. The identification of similarities despite methodological differences (C106-C107) is important for interpreting the relevance of the findings to human TMS-EEG studies. The interpretation is balanced and appropriately cautious.

result: PCI predicts consciousness by computing spatiotemporal complexity of EEG responses to brief brain stimulation pulses, with high sensitivity and specificity in individual patients. While spontaneous EEG has high false alarm/miss rates, PCI has been comprehensively validated in humans since 2005. Prior rodent PCI studies showed complexity differences between conscious and unconscious states, with down-states disrupting complex activation patterns during unconscious states. However, none simultaneously recorded neurons, LFP at hundreds of sites, and EEG.
evaluation: Claims C1-C17 provide appropriate background on PCI and prior work, all supported by extensive citations. C17 correctly identifies the novelty of the current study's multi-scale approach. These are primarily literature review claims that accurately represent prior work and appropriately motivate the current study.

result: Deep cortical stimulation in awake mice evokes a triphasic pattern (brief excitation, 120 ms off period, rebound excitation) locally and in thalamic nuclei, associated with a pronounced late EEG component. Cortico-thalamo-cortical interactions drive long-lasting evoked EEG signals during wakefulness. These responses are reduced during running and absent during anesthesia. Cortical stimulation elicits complex ERPs when awake but simpler ERPs when anesthetized, consistent with human and rodent studies.
evaluation: Claims C2-C5, C18-C20 represent the core findings of the manuscript, summarizing the main experimental results. These are well-supported by the comprehensive data presented throughout the paper (Figures 1-8). The inference about CTC interactions (C4, C20) is strongly supported by timing analysis and correlations, though the causal language ('drive', 'necessary') is somewhat stronger than the correlational data strictly support. Nevertheless, the evidence is compelling.

result: This study produced novel results linking ERPs to CTC loop activity. Rodent models offer unique opportunities to combine EEG with high-density recording to illuminate microcircuit dynamics. This work enables future studies using various perturbational techniques to causally link cell types, brain regions, and network dynamics to EEG signals and ERP features.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 appropriately summarize the study's contributions and implications. C108 is supported by the novel findings. C109 is a general statement about rodent models that is well-established. C110 appropriately identifies future directions, though the causal claims would require the suggested follow-up experiments.
